chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Fadhal, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from Ammar ibn Musa, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who catches a 'khattaf' in the desert or hunts it, [he asked]: Does he eat it? He said: 'It is among what is eaten.' And regarding the 'wabr', [he asked]: Is it eaten? He said: 'No, it is forbidden.'

His saying (peace be upon him) regarding the khattaf that 'it is among what is eaten' was intended as an expression of wonder/surprise at it, rather than intending to inform that it is permissible, because we have previously presented a narration indicating that it is not eaten. And this runs in the manner of one of us saying to another when he sees him eating something that the self dislikes: 'This is something that is eaten,' and he intends thereby to mock/ridicule him, not to inform him that it is permissible.

key_terms.الْخُطَّاف: A type of desert creature, often identified as a lizard or small reptile
key_terms.الْوَبْر: A type of desert creature, often identified as a scorpion or similar insect

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating khattaf and wabr in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the legal status of the 'khattaf' (likely a desert rodent) and 'wabr' (pika), distinguishing between linguistic surprise and definitive prohibition. The commentary highlights the Shia scholarly principle of reconciling apparent contradictions by interpreting the Imam's statement as rhetorical emphasis on edibility rather than a binding legal ruling, contrasting it with the explicit 'haram' status of the wabr. This reflects the broader jurisprudential approach of contextualizing prophetic and imamic speech within the framework of other corroborating texts.
